report.tagline: AI software that helps lawyers at big firms and companies research, draft and review legal documents faster.
report.simpleSummary: Harvey is an AI assistant built for lawyers. A lawyer can upload 500 contracts and ask 'which ones let the other side cancel early?' and get a table of answers with the exact clauses. It also drafts memos, checks documents and answers legal research questions. Big law firms and company legal teams pay for it per lawyer, every year.

overview.whatItDoes: Harvey is AI made for legal work. It helps lawyers read large piles of documents, draft contracts and memos, and research law across countries. It runs inside a secure workspace so client data stays private. It now also offers 'agents' that do multi-step tasks, like a first review of a deal's documents.
howItWorks: A firm signs a yearly contract and gives seats to its lawyers.
Lawyers use the Assistant to ask questions or draft text in plain English.
Vault lets them upload thousands of files and ask questions across all of them at once, with answers in a table.
Workflows and agents run set tasks, like drafting a client alert or checking a contract against a firm's rules.
Answers link back to the exact page or clause so lawyers can check.
Harvey plugs into Microsoft Word, Outlook and firm document systems, and partners with LexisNexis for case law.
overview.valueProposition: Do in an hour what used to take a junior lawyer a week, with sources you can check and data that stays private.

businessModel.summary: Harvey sells yearly subscriptions to law firms and company legal teams, priced per lawyer seat. Big firms sign large contracts. Revenue grows when firms add more lawyers or buy more products.

revenueStreams.detail: Yearly price per lawyer, with minimum seat counts for firms.
Large firm-wide or company-wide deals with custom workflows and support.
Vault, agents and premium content like LexisNexis may raise the price per seat.

businessModel.pricing: Not public. Reports suggest about $1,000 to $1,500 per lawyer per year, with minimum seat counts.
costDrivers: AI model costs from OpenAI, Anthropic and others
Large sales and customer success teams for big firms
In-house lawyers who build and test workflows
businessModel.unitEconomics: Rough example: a firm with 1,000 lawyers pays about $1.2M a year. If AI costs are about $200 to $300 per active lawyer a year and support costs are spread over many seats, Harvey keeps most of that. A lawyer bills about $500 or more an hour, so saving even 3 hours a year pays for the seat. The real cost is winning the deal: long pilots and big sales teams make CAC, the cost to win a customer, high.

howTheyGetUsers: Early deals with famous firms like Allen & Overy (now A&O Shearman), which made others follow
Direct sales to the top law firms and big companies
Partnerships with LexisNexis and big consulting firms
Land and expand: start with a pilot, then grow to the whole firm
whatBringsUsersBack: Custom firm workflows built inside Harvey
Vault projects that hold ongoing deal documents
Word and Outlook add-ins in the daily tools
growth.moat: Harvey's moat is trust and switching cost. Top firms already chose it, which signals safety to others. Firms build custom workflows inside it, so leaving means rebuilding. But the AI models underneath are available to rivals too.

pmLessons: In high-stakes work, trust beats features. Citations and privacy decided who won law firms.
Land famous early customers. One big-name firm convinced many others.
Seats sold is not the goal. Usage per seat decides if the customer renews.
Learn how your customer makes money. Firms bill by the hour, so faster work can hurt their income unless pricing changes.
Build workflows on top of AI models, because the models themselves are not unique.

interviewQuestions.question: Law firms bill by the hour. Why would they buy a tool that makes lawyers faster?
interviewQuestions.hint: Talk about client pressure for lower bills, fixed fees, competition between firms, and doing more work with the same staff. Show the incentive problem and how Harvey can help firms change pricing.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you increase usage among senior partners at a firm using Harvey?
interviewQuestions.hint: Segment users, find partner jobs (pitches, client updates), reduce effort with Outlook add-ins, and track weekly active partners.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure Harvey's answer quality?
interviewQuestions.hint: Combine expert audits, citation accuracy, accepted draft rate, and complaint tracking. Make hallucination rate a guardrail.

interviewQuestions.question: Thomson Reuters owns Westlaw. How does Harvey win against it?
interviewQuestions.hint: Compare content versus product speed. Discuss partnerships (LexisNexis), workflow depth and switching cost.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Harvey build its own AI model?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh cost and talent against control and margins. Most value is in data, workflows and trust. Suggest fine-tuning over building from scratch.
